summary:
What real-world issue are we addressing?

• Since we first started exploring space, we have lost and left many items on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. These can be anything from gloves, 2 golf balls and a feather, scientific instruments, heat shields, rovers and the Kepler telescope.


Why is it important?

• Before being abandoned, these machines contributed to remarkable discoveries, but their stories are not easily accessible particularly for younger people.

• Starting with the Kepler (K2) telescope, we have transformed these forgotten items into an engaging educational game, enabling young people discover the science, engineering and human achievements behind space exploration.
details:
Project ROFKA: summary of the proposed solution

The idea

Project ROFKA is a browser-based, open-world educational game about space debris and the machines humanity abandons in space. Players learn real science by examining genuine Earth hardware through the eyes of aliens who have only ever known humans by the junk that falls from their sky.

The story

An astronaut crew bound for Kepler-221b, a real exoplanet confirmed in 2014 using data from NASA's Kepler telescope, hits an event horizon and burns all its fuel escaping. The crew send a distress signal and go into cryo-sleep. The player wakes in the basement of Orryn, a Keplarian "archaeologist of the sky" who distrusts humans. Waking the crew and surviving depends on earning the trust of Kepler's inhabitants.

Core gameplay loop

  1. Inspect real space hardware as a 3D hologram you rotate and take apart: NASA's Kepler telescope, which leads into the K2 mission, and Telstar 1, a dead satellite still in orbit after radiation from the Starfish Prime nuclear test disabled it.
  2. Debate the Keplarians' mistaken theories, such as "it's a weapon" or "your kind abandons everything", by choosing the evidence that disproves each claim.
  3. Earn trust through a Trust Rank, which unlocks new areas, food and water, and stat points.

Areas

  • Orryn's archive: the tutorial, with the Kepler telescope.
  • The Hall of Fallen Craft (museum): Telstar 1 and real debris exhibits, including Vanguard 1, a lost spacewalk glove, a lost tool bag and a spent rocket stage.
  • The Veshari Market: a hostile crowd and a boss debate in the style of a typical video game, with Resolve, Toughness, weaknesses and an "Earthrise" ultimate. Winning unlocks four shops.
  • The Road to the Wilds: an open forest with a day/night cycle, wildlife and an Observation Notebook.

Game systems

  • Debate stats: Charisma, Intelligence and Critical Thinking. Critical Thinking also names the logical fallacy in each claim.
  • Stat-boosting food and cooking, plus survival meters for food, water and hygiene.
  • Technical knowledge and Earth Stories as currency: players are paid for sharing knowledge of everyday life on Earth.
  • Biology Level, separate from Trust Rank: players earn it by calmly observing wildlife over time to fill in 21 notebook entries.
  • Codex of the four Keplarian life forms.

Worldbuilding

Kepler's life comes in four "Great Forms", each built on a real area of science:

  • Hexarians: geometry, crystals and honeycombs.
  • Condensates: liquid–liquid phase separation in cells.
  • Folded Ones: protein folding.
  • Waveforms: electromagnetic waves and interference.

Kepler has no predators or prey; life there advances through mutual transformation. This contrasts with Earth, whose sky is cluttered with its own debris.

What players learn

  • Space debris: why it builds up, the risk of runaway collisions (Kessler syndrome), how the ISS dodges debris, retirement and de-orbit rules, and planned clean-up missions.
  • How real spacecraft work and why they fail.
  • The Outer Space Treaty, and why Earth matters (Pale Blue Dot, Earthrise).
  • Real biology and physics behind the alien life.
  • Critical thinking: spotting logical fallacies.

Every fact sits next to an in-world "real science" note, so players can always tell science from fiction.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Plays instantly in any modern browser on desktop, tablet or phone, with touch controls and no install or sign-in: nasa-project-rofka.netlify.app, with a QR code for posters.
  • Built as a single HTML file using Three.js. All dialogue, facts and debate content sit in one plain-text section, so team members without coding experience can edit them.

Possible next steps


More artifacts and factions beyond the ridge, waking the crew, Waveform concept art, and proper 3D character models, possibly moving to Unity or Godot.


NASA datasets

Every examinable artifact is a disused, discontinued, failed or retired project listed on NASA's catalog, with the first examinable artifact being Kepler's K2 telescope (which also acts as an important lore point in the context of the game).
